summary: Learners recognise that volume is additive: a composite solid made of non-overlapping right rectangular prisms has a total volume equal to the sum of its parts. The core skill is to decompose an L-shaped or step-shaped solid into cuboids, deduce any hidden dimension from the overall measurements, find each part's volume with V = l × w × h, and add — keeping consistent cubic units (typically cm³) throughout, matching the labelled measurements. Chief hazards are choosing overlapping pieces (double-counting the shared region), mis-reading or mis-deducing a missing dimension, and adding the parts wrongly or omitting one. A key insight is that any valid non-overlapping split of the same solid yields the same total.
misconceptions: Chooses overlapping pieces and double-counts the shared region.
Mis-deduces a hidden dimension (uses an overall length for a part, or forgets to subtract).
Adds the part-volumes incorrectly, or omits one of the parts.

activities.title: Pull the step-solid apart (exploded decomposition)
steps: Meet a step-shaped or L-shaped block with most edge lengths labelled and one or two left to deduce.
Draw a cut line to split the solid into two (or more) cuboids, then separate the pieces into an exploded view so you can see each one whole.
Check that your pieces do not overlap — no cube belongs to two pieces and none of the solid is left out.

Find any missing edge from the labelled measurements (for example, subtract the known part from the overall length, add parts to get an overall length, or use a matching parallel edge), then write down each cuboid's l, w and h.
Compute each cuboid's volume with V = l × w × h, keeping consistent cubic units (cm³ here), and add them for the total.
Re-split the same block a different valid way and confirm you get the same total.
activities.insight: Volume is additive: a composite solid can be decomposed into non-overlapping cuboids, each cuboid's volume found by l × w × h, and the parts summed — and any valid non-overlapping split rebuilds the same total.

activities.title: Decompose on a diagram with dimension deduction
steps: On a labelled L-shape diagram, draw split lines to divide it into non-overlapping cuboids.
Deduce each unlabelled dimension from the labelled ones (for example, by subtracting a known part from the overall measurement, adding parts, or matching an equal parallel edge), and write it in.
Compute each part's volume with l × w × h and add for the total, keeping consistent cubic units (cm³).
Try a second valid set of split lines and check the total is unchanged.
activities.insight: A composite solid's volume can be computed by splitting its diagram into non-overlapping rectangular prisms, deducing missing dimensions from the whole, and summing the parts.

activities.title: Real-world composite volume problem
steps: Read a real-world situation (e.g. a step-shaped concrete structure or an L-shaped container) with a labelled solid.
Decide how to split it into non-overlapping cuboids and deduce any missing dimension.
Calculate each part's volume and add for the total, giving the answer in consistent cubic units matching the labelled measurements (e.g. cm³ or m³).
State whether the total makes sense, and which part contributes the largest volume.
activities.insight: The additive-volume method applies to practical problems where a real object is modelled as a composite of rectangular prisms.

activities.title: Spot the overlap and the missing dimension (practice items)
steps: Work through short items that ask you to split an L-solid, find a missing length, and compute the total.
For each item, examine the answer choices and identify which come from double-counting an overlap and which from leaving a dimension un-deduced.
Explain, in one sentence, why your chosen split avoids counting any cube twice.
Construct at least one full split-and-sum yourself so you produce the method rather than only selecting an answer.
activities.insight: Recognising the specific error patterns — double-counting a shared region and mis-deducing a hidden dimension — supports more reliable use of the method; selecting a correct answer is not the same as producing a decomposition.

checkQuestion: Give a labelled L-shaped (or step-shaped) solid with most dimensions shown and one or two to be deduced. Say: 'Find its total volume, and show how you split it up.' Then WATCH whether they split into non-overlapping cuboids, how they find the missing dimension, whether they multiply each part correctly and add, and whether they double-count the overlap.
checkAnswer: Splits the solid into non-overlapping cuboids, deduces each missing dimension from the whole, computes each volume with l×w×h, and adds to the correct total in cm³ (splitting a different valid way gives the same answer).
